name: Communism
summary: Communism aims at a classless society in which the means of production are held in common, money and wage labour disappear, and goods are distributed according to need. Following Marx and Engels, it sees history as driven by class struggle and holds that capitalism must be overthrown by a working-class revolution. In its Marxist-Leninist form a vanguard party leads a transitional dictatorship of the proletariat that nationalises and plans the economy before the state is expected to wither away.
scope: Marxist communism as set out in the founding texts of Marx and Engels (the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Principles of Communism, the Civil War in France, the Critique of the Gotha Programme) and Lenin's State and Revolution, which the Marxist Internet Archive's entry on communism and the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of Marx present as its core: the abolition of private ownership of the means of production, a transitional proletarian state, and a stateless classless society distributing by need. The 1977 Soviet Constitution is used only as the written record of the ruling party and economic system in the Marxist-Leninist states. It excludes anarcho-communism, left and council communism, and the later practice of communist parties, which no saved record source covers.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Engels's Principles of Communism says that once all capital, production and exchange are in the hands of the nation, private property disappears and money becomes superfluous.

notes: Rebuilt under rules 7 on 2026-11-13. The earlier pass relied on Wikipedia articles and on the practice of ruling parties that no saved record source documents; every answer that rested on them, or that deduced a position from a general principle, was nulled and kept in reviewHistory, and 111 candidate statements were answered or left null. Themes searched in the saved texts: economy and property (Manifesto II, Principles, Gotha I-IV), state and government (State and Revolution III and V, Civil War in France), religion and morality (Manifesto II, Stanford Encyclopedia), family and gender, class and history, war and the nation. Lenin's texts on the national question and on defeat of one's own government (s7, s9, s11) are not tied to the ideology by the defining sources, so the national and war statements stay null; the three remain listed only because the review history of nulled answers cites them, and only s7 and s9 have saved copies. The Soviet constitutional record (Articles 6, 10, 40 and 52) answers four statements. Statements on environment, technology policy, migration, and modern social questions have no position in these texts.
